extracted.intended_audience: planters, overseers, and prospective lessees managing plantations (19th‑century American South)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for running a plantation: keeping plantation records, supervising labor (formerly enslaved people / freedmen), managing livestock and crops (especially cotton), contracting/leasing plantations, and organizing discipline and welfare. Emphasis on day-to-day operational rules and expected practices for an overseer/manager.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plantation record keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a daily and annual written record of all important events and business of the plantation using a prepared 'Plantation Record' book (daily work, picking progress, amounts picked by each person, monthly and yearly inventories of stock and tools, supplies received/distributed, lists of births and deaths, shipments, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books had blanks for every day of the year and for monthly/yearly inventories. On pages marked I the planter records all negroes with ages and 'cash value' at the beginning and end of the year, noting increases or deaths and transferring differences to the balance-sheet. Daily entries typically note labor performed, movements of stock and hands, punishments, health incidents, and other occurrences (examples include whip entries, jail fees, stocks, inventories, and holiday notes). Use the record to charge the crop with any depreciation in value due to overwork or to credit increases due to training or skill development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out employer's orders and study his interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The overseer is engaged to devote his time and energies for a year to carry out the orders of his employer strictly, cheerfully, and to the best of his ability, always studying and promoting the employer's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On entering duties, learn the condition of the plantation and the employer's views on management; if objections occur, state them clearly so they can be resolved. Treat the employer's trust as sacred; the overseer's fidelity to duties is expected as long as the employer is faithful to his part of the agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant presence and supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Remain constantly on the plantation and be with your people whenever they are present; constant oversight is the principal way to secure well-done work and to prevent idleness, theft, and disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for unavoidable business or attendance at Divine worship, the overlooker's continual presence is urged. When an overseer's back is turned much work will be slighted and opportunities for thieving will arise; correction after the fact often produces worse evils than prevention. Your paid time must be devoted to supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal conduct and expense management for the overseer
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid entertaining a constant run of company or incurring unnecessary expenses that take up the overseer's time or resources; keep household help only as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not have extraneous domestic arrangements (e.g., an extra woman to cook and wash) that increase expense and distract from duties. The overseer should take an interest in the place as if it were his own and be economical in private expenditures and hospitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care for health and well-being of laborers
rubrics_metrics.description: Overseers must attend to the health of laborers: prevent overwork and exposure, provide sufficient clothing and well-cooked food at regular hours, arrange indoor employment in wet weather, and ensure proper care of the sick, nursing mothers, and infants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommendations: have clothing ready in good season; provide profitable indoor employment in wet weather; supply an abundant diet of wholesome, well-cooked food including vegetables at regular hours; cheer and encourage the sick and provide extra comforts during convalescence; keep nursing women near the nursery but avoid breastfeeding when overheated; ensure infants are nursed three additional times during the day beyond morning and evening; never permit whisky on the place; while heated and at work, provide plenty of pure, cool water; guard against carrying heavy baskets on the head. Exert yourself to manage ordinary sickness; when beyond competence, send for a physician per owner's orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock and team management
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a reliable stock-minder/hostler, enforce a strict system in the care of animals, and make responsible persons answerable for animals, gear, and feed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put stables in good order and, if possible, lockable; appoint a steady, careful old man as hostler and make foremen directly answerable to him. Keep feed cut and ready, stalls clean, attend to sick or maimed animals, keep gear hung correctly and repaired. Proper stock-minding reduces overseer trouble and prevents waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding and work schedule for horses and mules
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain teams in good working condition economically by feeding appropriate green and dry feeds and limiting daily work hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheaper, effective feeds include oats, millet, peas (vine and all), broadcast corn, Bermuda/crab-grass hay, fed green when available, with a feed of dry oats, corn, or corn-chop at noon. Feed green shoots (oats/millet) or peas when budding and corn when tasselling. Keep teams to eight or nine hours of actual work per day for best performance and economy; rested teams perform more and are ready for strenuous 'push' work when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxen and cattle feeding and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain only as many work oxen as can be kept in good order and provide inexpensive but nutritious feeds; give special care to young stock and fatten/salvage aging animals properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide abundant green feed in spring/summer (cut and fed) and in winter feed well-boiled cotton-seed with a couple quarts of meal per head, turnips raw or cooked, corn-cobs soaked 24 hours in salt water, shucks, pea-vines passed through a cutting-box. Let calves have fair milk share and cooked food; fatten old or failing animals and save hides carefully (salt and dry) if killed for use. Fewer cattle are generally better unless range is exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hog management (avoid mismanagement and excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hogs are commonly mismanaged; avoid keeping too many and apply careful management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that hogs are generally sadly mismanaged and implies oversight on numbers and feeding is necessary (full guidance follows in subsequent text beyond this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotton-picking technique and labor allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cotton-picking is a skilled task favoring dexterity rather than brute strength; pickers walk between rows and collect bolls into shoulder bags, with usual allowances per hand per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pickers typically gather half the row on their right and half on their left; when stalks are low one person may take an entire row. A bag is suspended by a strap over the shoulder; skillful pickers remove the cotton by a single dextrous twist without touching the bolls to operate rapidly. Typical proper allowance is 100–400 pounds per hand per day depending on plant condition; stints under slavery fixed a day's quota under penalty. Picking season begins August/September and usually ends before Christmas; late seasons and rain reduce yields (example: 50–75 lbs/day in poor conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate measurement and accountability of labor (the 'tell-tale')
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighing each basket and recording individual daily yields increases accountability and worker effort, exposing deception and improving productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'tell-tale' (scales/overseer who weighs baskets) removed opportunity for deception about quantities picked. After introducing weighing and daily announcements of results, worker performance improved noticeably. Record daily amounts on slate and transfer to account book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lease contract terms for cultivating abandoned plantations
rubrics_metrics.description: When leasing plantations, formalize terms in a contract covering duration, responsibilities, shares of current and future crops, supervision, removal of tools and stock, and condition of return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical private leases: lessee gathers crops then standing, sells current cotton and needed corn, cultivates best ability subject to flood/fire/war/marauders, returns plantations at year end in as good condition regarding stock/tools unless prevented by circumstances beyond control, furnishes stock/tools with privilege to remove them upon departure, and has full supervision. Example negotiated splits: owner to have half current crops and varying shares of the year's product (one-fourth to one-third or seven twenty-fourths in an example). Government leases required additional formalities and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider military protection and government assistance when leasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess promises of military protection and the likelihood of government support (posts, cavalry patrols) when taking leases on abandoned plantations; protection affects feasibility and risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents promised military posts at points along the river, stockades, and cavalry patrols to protect plantations and relieve authorities of responsibility for freedpeople. Such protection was presented as part of a policy to foster enterprise and employ freedmen as free laborers; verify promised protection and its geographic coverage before leasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of wage/payment system and its effect on labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a payment scheme carefully: share-of-product with supplied rations, monthly wages with withheld pay, or daily wages with immediate pay each night—each system produces different incentives for waste, industry, and frugality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed outcomes: (1) share system where owners furnish food/clothing and divide income encourages waste and idleness because laborers are not liable for supplies; (2) monthly wages with half withheld fosters somewhat more industry but delayed payment inhibits economy; (3) daily wages with money paid at night and laborers buying their own rations promotes frugality and greater industry as workers are directly responsible for expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand causes of theft and design management to reduce it
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that petty theft and deception among laborers often stem from lack of compensation, scant rations, and the prior system of slavery; management should address underlying causes rather than only punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System of slavery left laborers with no compensation beyond subsistence, incentivizing theft of food items. Most petty thefts were to supply personal wants. Remedies include fair compensation, adequate rations, attentive supervision, and humane treatment to reduce incentives to steal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and punishment practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments (whippings, stocks, jail) were commonly recorded and used; their frequency and severity varied by overseer and could be moderated by authorities when excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plantation records show routine whippings, use of dogs to hunt runaways, jail fees, stocks, and other punishments. Overseers differ—some rarely whipped, others often. When local freedmen courts or authorities impose severe sentences, higher authorities may need to modify them. Discipline practices should be recorded and administered in accordance with employer and governmental orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and supervise local freedmen courts for petty offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Create courts with local freedmen (judge, jury, counsel, officers) to adjudicate petty cases like theft and fraud, as an educational tool for self-government, but ensure oversight and moderation of sentences by supervisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Davies' Bend a negro court tried petty cases with all black officers; punishments decreed were often severe and required modification by authorities. The experiment aimed to teach freedmen self-governance but required careful watching and was opposed by planters who disliked elevating the black population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage social arrangements of laborers (marriage policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plantation owners often discouraged official marriages among laborers because marriages complicated saleability of the working force; overseers recorded and sometimes controlled relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example record: owner did not approve of marriages, but permitted cohabitation; entries in plantation records recorded requests to marry and owners' refusals. Overseers should note owner's policy and enforce it according to instructions.
